1:
Why the consecration is narrated here, after seven chapters of sacrificial law, two of them answer alike. Ellicott points out that the rite was to be accompanied by several kinds of offering, so the ritual of each had to be defined before the ceremony could be described; that done, the lawgiver simply resumes the narrative broken off at the close of Exodus. Keil and Delitzsch put it structurally: the command was received on the mountain with the instructions for building the sanctuary, but could not be executed until the institution of sacrifice was in place, since most of the sacrificial laws bear upon this act. They also sketch what follows — consecration by investiture, anointing and sacrifice here; solemn entrance upon office next; and the sanctifying of that priesthood by judgment on Aaron's eldest sons after that.

When the words were spoken is disputed. Gill reports Jarchi's view that this paragraph was delivered a week before the tabernacle went up, and rejects it: the preceding chapters were spoken out of the tabernacle, which argues that it stood already, and the order for consecration was renewed once the sacrificial laws had been given, precisely so that the new priests might have something to offer. Calvin goes further and rearranges the material. The carrying out of this command belongs, he says, to another moment — the solemn dedication of the tabernacle — and he has therefore moved his own treatment of it to that place, so that the history may run on uninterrupted.

Henry gives the same reasons for the delay in homelier terms. A newly erected tabernacle without priests would be a candlestick without a candle; a newly given law of sacrifice could not be kept without them; and though Aaron and his sons had been nominated already, they could not officiate until consecrated, which had to wait until their place of ministry was ready and the ordinances instituted — so that they might set to work the moment they were ordained, and understand that they were ordained not merely to honour and profit but to the business of the priesthood. Clarke marks the same distinction more briefly: until now the thing had only been commanded, and here it is first performed.

That Moses was consecrating his own relations is a delicacy Henry and Gill both notice. Henry observes that Aaron and his sons stood near to Moses in blood, and that he therefore would not consecrate them without further orders, lest he seem too forward in bringing honour into his family. Gill makes the record itself the proof: Moses sets down the command so as to show he acted under divine warrant, not out of favour and affection for a brother, and to show that Aaron did not take the honour to himself.

The materials to be brought are itemised, and Ellicott corrects the article. Not a bullock and two rams and a basket, but the bullock, the two rams and the basket — the very offering prescribed in Exodus, which he takes as evidence of how intimately this part of Leviticus hangs on the close of that book. The garments likewise are the ones God had already ordered to be made.

Calvin adds a note on the priest's own meal offering. Besides the sacrifice of consecration a second oblation was demanded of him, a cake fried in a pan and cut in pieces, the reason being that he might become the lawful minister of all the people and offer in another's name only after doing what was right for himself. One difference from the people's offering he thinks worth explaining: the priest's was wholly burnt. Had it been kept for his use, as the people's remainder was kept for theirs, it might easily have become an occasion of vain ostentation, and God was unwilling to leave that door open.
3:
Nobody supposes that the whole nation stood in the courtyard. Gill takes the summons, on Aben Ezra's reading, for the heads of the tribes and the elders, since every individual could not possibly be got together. Ellicott would render the word assembly rather than congregation, as the next verse already does, and identifies it with the elders, heads of tribes and principal men who represented the people — a reading he confirms from the following chapter, where Moses calls Aaron, his sons and the elders of Israel, and where those same elders are then called the children of Israel precisely because they stood for them. He would also correct the venue: not the door of the tabernacle of the congregation but the entrance of the tent of meeting, meaning its courtyard.

Wesley allows a larger crowd than that. The elders represented everyone, but as many of the people as wished and could reach the place came too, so that all might witness both Aaron's commission from God and the work it committed him to. Ellicott arrives at much the same picture by geography: the representatives and as many more as the enclosure would conveniently hold stood inside, while those who wanted to see the ceremony probably occupied the neighbouring ground overlooking it. He adds a date from tradition current in the time of Christ, which placed the ceremony on the twenty-third of Adar.

Calvin explains why he has handled the material here rather than earlier. The priesthood's authority and nature he expounded under the Second Commandment; but these chapters are historical, and had he taken them up with the commandment, inexperienced readers would not have easily noticed when they belonged. Keeping them apart lets those readers see, once the doctrine proper to the Decalogue has been set out, how faithfully Moses performed what he was commanded, and compare the obedience with the injunction just as they could through the making and dedication of the tabernacle. That the narrative must be connected in this way he thinks beyond question, since many passages make it plain that the priests were anointed on the same day the tabernacle was consecrated.

What Moses actually did is reported with an eye to his warrant. Gill has him convene Aaron, his sons and the heads of the people, and come himself bringing the garments, the oil and the sacrifices — everything the consecration required; Ellicott makes the same point, that the summons was only half the errand, the vestments and victims having to be fetched as well. When Moses spoke, Gill notes, he opened the reason for the gathering, and did so not of himself but by divine direction; Ellicott identifies the words he published as the instructions already recorded in Exodus. Calvin sees the bringing near as a setting of the men before God and the people at once.
6:
The first act is a bath, and it is taken to mean more than cleanliness. Keil and Delitzsch read the washing as directed rather than performed by Moses — he told them to wash themselves, all over and not merely hands and feet — and treat the removal of bodily uncleanness as a symbol of putting away the filth of sin, without which nobody could approach God, and least of all men whose office was to perform the duties of reconciliation. Ellicott reaches the same sense philologically: where the phrase to wash with water is used without naming any part of the body it denotes bathing the whole of it, as several passages show. Gill locates the act at the laver standing in the court.

Where the bathing happened Ellicott is careful about, and his answer shapes the verse that follows. It was not done in sight of the people but behind a curtain, in what he calls a baptistry; and he adds from later practice that under the second Temple the priestly immersion could not be managed in any vessel but had to take place in a hollow cut in the ground holding at least twenty-four cubic feet of water. He notes one further transfer of function: the installation performed here by Moses, as giver and representative of the divine law, was in that later period carried out by the Sanhedrin, who sat in Moses' seat.

A garment named in Exodus is missing from the list here, and Gill and Ellicott explain the omission identically. The linen drawers, being nearest the skin, were not among the things Moses put on Aaron; the man dressed himself in them privately — behind the curtain immediately after his bath, Ellicott says; in some apartment of the tabernacle or before he ever came, Gill suggests — since it would not have been decent to have them put on in the sight of the whole assembly.

The rest of the vesting is set out garment by garment, and Ellicott separates two things the English blurs. The girdle first mentioned is not the band of the ephod but the needlework belt with which the tunic was gathered at the loins; the curious girdle named afterwards is better simply the band, woven out of the same piece as the ephod on either side, so that the garment had as it were two hands which made up the band. He describes the ephod as the high priest's distinctive vestment, sleeveless and worn over the shoulders, of blue and purple and scarlet and fine twined linen shot with gold; the robe beneath it as the seamless, wholly blue robe of the ephod; and the coat as a tunic. Gill runs through the same sequence, noting that the linen coat lay next the flesh and that the garments went on in exactly the order the text gives them.

Keil and Delitzsch supply the meaning of the whole operation in a sentence. Putting on an official dress of this importance signified endowment with the character the office required, the costume being the outward sign of installation in the post its wearer was to fill.

Two items are treated as distinct from the garments carrying them. Gill describes the breastplate as made of the same materials as the ephod, laid on it and fastened to it, and Ellicott adds its fuller title, the breastplate of judgment, another distinctively pontifical piece of the same costly stuff and skilful work. About what went inside it both he and Clarke are explicit: the Urim and the Thummim were something separate from the breastplate itself and from the gems set in it, and the verb means that Moses put them into its bag. Of the mitre Gill says only what it was — fine linen, wound at considerable length about the head.
10:
The oil goes first to the building and its furniture. Gill notes that Bezaleel had compounded it on directions Moses received from the Lord. Ellicott lists what it touched — ark, altar of incense, candlestick, table of shewbread and every utensil belonging to them — and defines the sanctifying: the unction separated them from common use and dedicated them to God, so that they were thereafter to touch no defilement.

The sevenfold sprinkling of the brazen altar is unexplained, and Gill says so. No direction about sprinkling, or a number of times, appears in the earlier legislation, and Jarchi confesses he does not know how these sprinklings were ordered; Gill assumes Moses was instructed of God and suggests the seven marks a perfect unction, making the altar a fitter type of Christ, who received the Spirit without measure. Ellicott confirms the rite is absent from the Exodus directions, and draws out the altar's new standing: once sanctified it was held to sanctify what was offered on it, which is the point of Christ's question whether the gift or the altar that sanctifies it is greater.

Aaron himself is treated differently, and all four notice it. Where the furniture was sprinkled, Wesley observes, the oil was poured on the high priest plentifully, because his unction typified the anointing of Christ with a Spirit not given him by measure — of which, he adds, every believer receives a measure. Gill traces the flow: down to the beard and the collar of the robe, not, as the English wrongly has it, to the skirts of his garments. Both then report a tradition about what followed the pouring, and the two differ: Jarchi and Maimonides have the anointer draw the oil between the eyebrows in the shape of a Greek chi, while the practice Ellicott records from the second Temple made it a Caph, the initial of the word for priest. Ellicott adds the standing distinction: every successor to the high priesthood was anointed by this profuse pouring, whereas ordinary priests were simply marked on the forehead at their first installation, that anointing serving their descendants ever after.

Aaron's sons are then brought forward, Gill naming all four: having consecrated the father, Ellicott says, Moses invested Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar with the visible signs of the office by robing them. Keil and Delitzsch look ahead to the closing sacrifices, noting two things. The victims were provided not by the men being installed but by Moses at the congregation's charge, the priesthood being instituted for them; and Moses, as mediator of the covenant, performed every part himself — slaughtering, sprinkling the blood, burning the altar gifts — exactly as the priests would afterwards.

Calvin explains why oil at all. Without the Spirit's influence every sacrifice would be unsavoury, and it was by that same Spirit that Christ was made peace-maker between God and men, a dignity not otherwise belonging to flesh and human nature. On the hands laid upon the victim he is equally exact: the gesture was not merely presentation but a testimony that guilt had been transferred, the private worshipper casting his sin upon the beast which then bore God's curse in his stead.

Why only one side of the body was stained with blood Calvin raises and declines to press. He warns against wanting to know more than Scripture reveals, calling such curiosity frivolous and perverse, then offers what he thinks probable: the whole body was consecrated in the right side, hands and feet standing for a man's entire life and actions. Why the ear and not the tongue he answers from the office. This consecration was not to teaching but to intercession, and the chief virtue obtaining grace in sacrifice is obedience — which is why the psalm says the ears have been opened where sacrifice was not desired, and why Moses began there.
14:
Henry explains why a consecration needs victims. The covenant of priesthood, like other covenants, had to be made by sacrifice — and so Christ was consecrated by the sacrifice of himself, once for all. He finds a pastoral reason in the requirement that offerings of every kind be made for the priests themselves: men who had stood beside their own sin offering would afterwards present the people's gifts with more tenderness, having compassion on the ignorant and those out of the way rather than insulting over them, remembering that they too were compassed with infirmity. The bullock, being the largest victim, was chosen so that atonement might be made and none of the guilt of their former condition carried into the office they were entering. Ministers who declare pardon to others, Henry adds, should be diligent to have their own sins pardoned first, and those charged with the ministry of reconciliation must be reconciled themselves before they deal for other men's souls.

Ellicott makes the same point from the ceremony's logic: duly consecrated though they were, Aaron and his sons had to be purged before they could begin priestly work, so that while Moses acted as the delegated mediator and performed the sacrificial rites, the new priests stood beside the victim as penitent sinners. Keil and Delitzsch note the rank of the animal — a young ox, the highest kind of sacrificial beast, matching the position the priesthood was to hold as the elect of the covenant nation.

Whether this was one bullock or seven exercises two of them. Clarke states plainly that the sin offering was repeated on each of the seven days of consecration; Wesley reconciles that with a text naming only one, observing that Moses is describing the first day's work alone.

Who wielded the knife is settled by the men's status. Gill points out that neither Aaron nor his sons could do it, not yet being fully consecrated, so Moses killed the beast; Ellicott confirms that although the offerer ordinarily slaughtered his own victim, Exodus had expressly assigned the act to Moses here.

What was done with the blood is described two ways. Keil and Delitzsch have Moses put some of it with his finger on the horns of the altar of burnt offering and pour the remainder at its base, and explain the departure from the usual rule: ordinarily the blood of a sin offering whose flesh was burnt outside the camp went into the sanctuary itself, but here it stayed on the brazen altar in order to make this offering a consecration sacrifice, purifying and sanctifying and expiating the altar. Ellicott has him catch the blood in a bowl and throw it on the four corners, and is emphatic about where it did not go — not to the horns of the incense altar or into the tent, as with the sin offerings for high priest and nation. He draws the parallel that governs the whole rite: as the priest was consecrated by the anointing oil and then purified by an expiatory sacrifice, so was the altar.

The disposal of the carcase follows the same divided pattern. Gill identifies the fat on the inwards by its anatomical name and reports Aben Ezra's two opinions about the burning outside the camp — that Moses did it, or that he gave the order, which Gill thinks likelier. Ellicott explains why nobody ate it, though the blood never entered the sanctuary and the offering therefore fell outside the usual rule: Moses could not, not being a legally consecrated priest, and the priests could not, the law forbidding a sinner to partake of the sin offering he had himself brought. Wesley notices the one part treated differently here from ordinary practice — the hide, which in offerings made for the people was not burnt but given to the priest.
18:
The second victim answers a different purpose from the first, and Keil and Delitzsch mark the transition. The sin offering had expiated priests and altar together and removed every disturbance of the fellowship between a holy God and the men who were to serve him at that altar — a disturbance caused, they point out, by the sin of the very men now being installed; a burnt offering follows, and it is carried out by the ordinary burnt-offering ritual. Ellicott says the same and adds the one departure from that ritual — Moses performed the priestly acts himself, where the rules of the first chapter assume a serving priest. Gill notes only that the ram was one of the two Moses had been ordered to take at the outset, the other being reserved for the consecration offering that follows. Ellicott fixes the sequence exactly: it was after their sins had been expiated by the sin offering that Moses could present this second victim on the new priests' behalf.

What the offering expressed Wesley supplies. By it the new priests gave God the glory of the great honour just put upon them, and signified at the same time the devoting of themselves and of all their service to him — the whole victim going up in smoke, as a burnt offering does, rather than being shared out between altar and worshipper.

Who killed the beast is a small question with a careful answer. Gill has Moses do it, citing the Greek version, and Ellicott agrees that although the offerer ordinarily slaughtered his own victim, Moses acted here as he had at the sin offering. Wesley leaves room for a deputy. The verb may mean Moses, as the following clause certainly does, or some other person acting by his appointment — and he finds a reason for the vagueness in what comes next, since the text does name Moses for the sprinkling of the blood, an act more properly priestly and more essential to the sacrifice than the killing.

Ellicott catches one more distinction the English loses. Where the Authorised Version has Moses sprinkle the blood, the Hebrew word is not the one used at the sin offering a few verses earlier; cast is the better rendering here. Gill follows the butchery through in his usual plain way: the head struck off and the carcase quartered, the inwards drawn and the legs severed, and both of those washed in water before they went to the fire.
22:
What the third victim is called, and why, occupies all four. Gill renders the name filling, or fulnesses, and reports Jarchi's explanation that these offerings filled and perfected the priests in their priesthood, this being the finishing and consummation of the whole consecration. Keil and Delitzsch agree that the ram was in form a peace offering and derive the title from the peculiar ceremony performed with its flesh, which turned the sacrifice into a consecration offering by inducting the men into possession and enjoyment of the priestly privileges; they note that a ram served as peace offering for the nation as a whole, for the tribe-princes, and for a Nazarite. Ellicott approaches it from the worshippers' side: the concluding sacrifice, resembling in form both thank offering and peace offering, was meant to express the gratitude Aaron and his sons felt at being chosen to the office, and their peace and fellowship with God.

The blood placed on the extremities is read as instruction. Ellicott takes the tip of the right ear to teach the high priest that, standing as mediator between God and the people, he was bound to hearken to the Lord's commandments; the thumb of the right hand to remind him that he was henceforth to execute God's will and walk in the way of those commandments. Why the right side rather than the left he answers practically — the right members are represented as the stronger, and so the fitter to carry out what God requires. He also notes that the same parts of the body were touched with blood when a cured leper was restored, and that Moses, having performed these acts upon the high priest, repeated them upon his four sons.

Ellicott also corrects one term among the portions handed over: not the fat and the rump but the fat and the fat-tail, the broad tail of the eastern sheep being reckoned among the choice pieces.

Clarke goes outside Scripture altogether for his comment, and the comparison is the most striking thing in the chapter. Following Calmet, he observes that the making of a Roman high priest bore a considerable resemblance to this rite. The candidate, robed in silk and crowned with gold and sacred ribbons, was led down into a pit roofed over with planks bored through with many holes; a bullock was killed on the boards above, and its blood ran down through the perforations upon the man beneath, who turned his whole body to the shower — face, eyes, nose, lips and even his tongue — so as to be completely covered. Coming up drenched, he was acknowledged and adored by the people as supreme high priest.

What Clarke makes of the parallel is worth stating exactly, since it runs the other way from what a reader might expect. He does not treat the Hebrew rite as a variant of the pagan one; he judges the Roman ceremony to bear a striking allusion to the consecration of Aaron, to have probably been borrowed from it, and then to have been disguised by the introduction of their own superstitions. For the details he cites the fourth-century poet Prudentius, whose description he quotes at length and whom he takes to have been intimately acquainted with what he was describing.
26:
The wave offering is described chiefly by who held what. Gill has Moses take from the basket the unleavened bread he had been ordered to bring, lay it with the fat and the right shoulder upon the hands of Aaron and his sons, and then take the whole back from their hands once it had been waved before the Lord. Clarke refers the nature of the waving and the heaving to his fuller treatment of the same rite in Exodus, without repeating it here.

The breast raises the question of wages. Ellicott explains that the breast-piece, which afterwards belonged by right to whichever priest officiated, fell on this occasion to Moses, in accordance with the direction given in Exodus, so that it served as his sacrificial meal — he being the man divinely appointed to perform the priestly service on that day. Wesley states the principle behind it more bluntly still: Moses was administering the priest's office at the time, and was therefore to receive the priest's wages.

The closing act mixes two things that had been kept separate, and how far they were mixed nobody can say. Gill notices that the oil and the blood from the altar seem to have been combined, the wording running them together. Ellicott is more cautious and more explicit about the limits of the evidence: some of the blood of the consecration ram was probably kept in the bowl and set on the altar for this purpose, but whether the anointing oil and the blood were sprinkled separately or mingled first cannot possibly be gathered either from this verse or from the passage in Exodus which prescribes the rite.

What was sprinkled, and on whom, both draw comment. Ellicott observes that the sacred garments received the same cleansing and sanctification as the men who wore them, since the vestments were the badge of the office — which is the sort of thing behind the apostle's remark that almost all things are by the law purged with blood. Clarke fastens on the person rather than the clothing. That the high priest himself had to be sprinkled with sacrificial blood he takes as a type discharged in Christ, who was sprinkled with his own: in the agony in the garden, in the crowning with thorns, in the piercing of hands and feet, and in the opening of his side with the spear — four acts of atonement performed, on Clarke's reading, by the high priest himself.
31:
Henry marks the handover: Moses having finished his part, Aaron and his sons do theirs, boiling the flesh of the peace offering and eating it in the court, burning whatever is left. He reads the meal as their thankful consent to the consecration, comparing Ezekiel, who at his commission was told to eat the roll. Ellicott specifies what was left to eat — all but the fat parts and right shoulder burnt on the altar and the wave-breast awarded to Moses — and corrects the venue to the entrance of the tent of meeting, that is, the court. Wesley notes that Moses handed his own portion to Aaron, so that he and his sons might eat it in token that they, and only they, should have that right in future.

Two features distinguish this meal from an ordinary peace offering, and Ellicott names both. It had to be eaten with unleavened bread, and no layman could share it — where at common sacrificial feasts the offerer might invite family and even strangers, here the flesh and bread were peculiarly holy, the sacrifice carrying the same atoning virtue as a burnt offering. Gill and Ellicott agree on the disposal of leftovers: nothing might be kept past the day, and whatever remained went into the fire.

Seven days indoors is the next requirement, and draws the fullest reflection. Calvin calls the rest of the ritual the universal rule and singles this out as the one special thing: God kept them in the tabernacle a week so that they might learn to subordinate every domestic care and worldly business to their sacred duties, and the number reminded them that for the rest of their lives they were no longer their own masters. Clarke says seven was the Hebrew number of perfection and takes the week to imply a perfect and full consecration. Henry gets a soldier's lesson — the priesthood being a good warfare, they must learn to endure hardness and disentangle themselves from the affairs of this life, as the apostles were afterwards appointed to wait for the promise of the Father.

How literally the confinement was meant is where Gill grows practical. Jewish writers, he reports, are puzzled where the men were to relieve themselves, the place being holy; Gill answers that the order cannot have been so strict as to forbid going in and out at all, only to forbid lingering or attending other business. Some had always to be on the spot keeping the Lord's charge, which implies turns; and they must have slept alternately, since they could no more go a week without rest than without food. Ellicott confines them to the court rather than the tent, the consecration having been performed at the entrance and not within.

That the whole ceremony was repeated daily three of them state. Keil and Delitzsch take the words to imply the rite in all its details was performed again for seven days; Ellicott spells out what that meant: sin offering, burnt offering and consecration offering each day, the men and their garments sprinkled afresh with blood and oil. Henry finds doctrine in the repetition. It shows the imperfection of legal sacrifices, repeated because they could not take away sin, and repeated here seven times, a number of perfection, because they typified the one offering that perfected for ever those who are sanctified.

One ambiguity Wesley leaves open: the he who consecrates may be God or Moses, since Moses often speaks of himself in the third person. Henry presses the charge itself. They attended day and night, and so constant should our meditation be; they attended to keep the charge of the Lord, and every one of us has a charge to keep — kept, as the text says, that you die not, since it is death, eternal death, to betray the trust we are charged with.
34:
The instruction to repeat everything is stated flatly and glossed the same way by both who take it up. Gill has the whole ceremony performed again on each of the remaining days until the seven were out, and cites Jarchi and Aben Ezra for it, adding that Jarchi reports a rabbinic gloss referring the verb in the preceding clause to the business of the red heifer. Ellicott improves the rendering — as hath been done this day, rather than as he hath done — and states the sense plainly: the rites gone through on the first day the Lord commanded to be repeated every day for a week.

Where exactly the men were to stay Gill settles on a preposition. The English leaves it open whether they abode outside the entrance or within, but since they were forbidden to go out of the door at all, he prefers Noldius's rendering, within it. What they actually did is reported in a sentence: they submitted to have done to them, and for them, on all the remaining days what had been done on the first, and they kept inside the tabernacle the whole time as they had been enjoined.

Clarke reads the closing verse as a receipt. The chapter shows the exact fulfilment of the commands delivered in Exodus, and therefore the complete preparation of Aaron and his sons to fill what he calls the awfully important office of priests and mediators between God and Israel, offering sacrifice and making atonement for the people's sins. He then quotes Ainsworth at length on what that priesthood was and what it lacked. The covenant confirmed to Levi in Aaron and his sons was one of life and peace; yet these men were made priests without an oath, and there had to be many of them, since death would not suffer them to continue. They served the example and shadow of heavenly things, offering gifts that could not perfect the worshipper as pertaining to the conscience, carnal ordinances imposed only until the time of reformation — until Christ, made priest with an oath and surety of a better covenant established on better promises, who because he continues for ever holds a priesthood that does not pass from one man to another, ministers in the true tabernacle God pitched and not man, and entered the holy place once by his own blood rather than the blood of bulls and goats, having found everlasting redemption and being able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him.

Wesley makes the same contrast in three sentences, saying that the covenant of life and peace was made with Aaron and his sons, and that after every ceremony used in their consecration one point was still reserved for the honour of Christ's priesthood — they were made priests without an oath, but Christ with an oath.

Clarke closes with the sharpest statement of the chapter's whole logic. Taken in reference to Christ's priesthood and sacrifice, he says, all these rites and ceremonies are significant and edifying; taken out of that relation they would be as absurd and nugatory as the blood-drenched making of a Roman high priest which he had described earlier from Prudentius.
